questions.text: What guidance does the comparison provide architects for communicating service distinctions to clients?

options.text: Architects must clearly communicate service distinctions to establish appropriate engagement arrangements and manage client expectations
The comparison indicates that service distinctions are too technical to explain to clients, which is a misconception
Architects should avoid clarifying service differences to clients, which could lead to misunderstandings
Client communication about service types is not relevant according to the comparison, which is misleading

rationale.b: Dismisses communication responsibility—the comparison explicitly mandates architects must clearly communicate distinctions to clients.
rationale.c: Contradicts professional duty—the comparison identifies clear communication about service types as essential, not something to avoid.
rationale.d: Denies communication importance—the comparison places client communication about service types as a core introductory professional requirement.
rationale.correct: The comparison introduction states 'Architects must clearly communicate these distinctions to clients to establish appropriate engagement arrangements' as a core professional responsibility.
rationale.takeaway: Architects must clearly communicate supervision vs. CM vs. administration distinctions to clients—this clarity establishes appropriate engagement arrangements and prevents scope misunderstandings.

questions.text: How does Article 1723 liability apply across the three service models according to the comparison?

options.text: Article 1723 applies to supervisors and construction managers directing structural work, establishing liability for technical decisions affecting structural integrity
The comparison indicates Article 1723 applies uniformly across all service models regardless of role, ensuring consistent accountability
Article 1723 applies exclusively to design services and not to supervision or management, limiting liability to architects
Limitation of authority completely exempts professionals from Article 1723 liability, provided they have documented disclaimers

rationale.b: Overstates uniformity—the comparison specifically ties Article 1723 to supervisors and CMs 'directing structural work,' not all roles equally.
rationale.c: Incorrectly narrows applicability—the comparison explicitly applies Article 1723 to supervisors and CMs when they direct structural decisions.
rationale.d: Falsely exempts through limitation—the comparison states limitations protect 'when operating within defined scope,' but doesn't claim to exempt Article 1723 entirely.
rationale.correct: The comparison states 'Article 1723 structural liability applies to supervisors and construction managers directing structural work' and identifies this as a key legal responsibility consideration.
rationale.takeaway: Article 1723 applies when supervisors or CMs direct/approve structural work—not uniform across all roles; it attaches to specific technical structural decision-making.

questions.text: What distinguishes SPP 202 Design Administration from the other service models?

options.text: Design Administration integrates design decisions with construction execution and post-occupancy support across all project phases
SPP 202 Administration is identical to full-time supervision services, offering no unique benefits or distinctions
Design Administration is only applicable to construction phase services, limiting its scope and applicability
The comparison indicates SPP 202 has no distinct characteristics from other models, making it redundant

rationale.b: Overstates similarity—the comparison explicitly distinguishes Design Administration as a comprehensive model spanning multiple phases and integrating design with construction.
rationale.c: Incorrectly narrows scope—the comparison identifies Design Administration as encompassing 'preliminary, design, construction, and post-construction' services, not construction-only.
rationale.d: Denies distinct model characteristics—the comparison explicitly establishes Design Administration as a distinct integrated model different from supervision or standalone CM.
rationale.correct: The comparison establishes Design Administration as the model that 'encompasses preliminary services, design phase services, construction phase services, and post-construction services' and 'integrates design decisions with construction execution and post-occupancy support.'
rationale.takeaway: SPP 202 Design Administration (SPP 202) spans all project phases from concept through post-occupancy—the most comprehensive engagement model, integrating design with construction and operations.

questions.text: In terms of authority scope, how do supervisors differ from construction managers according to the comparison?

options.text: Supervisors exercise technical compliance verification authority only; construction managers hold broader authority over scheduling, costs, and vendor coordination
Both supervisors and construction managers have identical authority over all project decisions, which is rarely the case in practice
Construction managers are limited to technical verification like supervisors, which is a misunderstanding of their role
The comparison indicates that authority scope is irrelevant to service distinctions, which is not typically accurate

rationale.b: Denies authority distinction—the comparison explicitly identifies supervisors' authority as 'limited to technical matters' versus CMs' 'broader authority.'
rationale.c: Misrepresents CM authority—the comparison explicitly establishes CM authority as 'broader' and extending to business decisions supervisors cannot make.
rationale.d: Denies authority significance—the comparison explicitly uses authority distinctions as a key differentiator among service models.
rationale.correct: The comparison states Supervisors 'exercise authority limited to technical compliance verification' while CMs 'hold broader authority over scheduling, cost management, and vendor coordination within owner-defined limits.'
rationale.takeaway: Supervisor authority is limited to technical compliance verification; CM authority extends to scheduling, costs, and vendor coordination—fundamentally different decision-making scopes.

questions.text: According to the comparison, why is authority clarification essential among these service models?

options.text: Authority clarification prevents role confusion and establishes clear responsibility boundaries among different service types
The comparison indicates that authority clarification is unnecessary since all models are identical in terms of their operational framework
Authority distinctions are irrelevant to contract negotiations, as they do not impact the legal enforceability of agreements
Contracts should avoid specifying authority limitations according to the comparison, to maintain flexibility in service delivery

rationale.b: Denies distinction necessity—the comparison explicitly identifies authority clarification as preventing confusion, implying distinctions exist.
rationale.c: Denies contract importance—the comparison emphasizes contracts 'must explicitly define authority limitations' for protection.
rationale.d: Contradicts contract requirement—the comparison states contracts 'must explicitly define authority limitations,' not avoid doing so.
rationale.correct: The comparison states 'Authority clarification prevents role confusion and establishes clear responsibility boundaries' and 'Contracts must explicitly define authority limitations to protect all parties.'
rationale.takeaway: Clear authority definition is essential because service models differ significantly—explicit contracts prevent role confusion and liability disputes among supervision, CM, and administration.

questions.text: How does the scope of Construction Management services differ from Full-Time Supervision according to the comparison?

options.text: Construction Management encompasses schedule progression, cost control, multi-trade coordination, and resource management beyond supervision's quality focus
Construction Management and Full-Time Supervision have identical scopes and responsibilities, with no distinctions in their roles
Construction Management is limited exclusively to quality verification like supervision, without involvement in other project aspects
The comparison indicates no functional differences between these service types, suggesting they are interchangeable

rationale.b: Denies scope distinction—the comparison explicitly identifies CM as 'broader' scope than supervision and lists distinct CM responsibilities.
rationale.c: Overly narrows CM scope—the comparison explicitly establishes CM as encompassing schedule, cost, coordination, and resource management beyond quality focus.
rationale.d: Denies critical distinctions—the comparison establishes key functional differences in authority, responsibility, and compensation methods between the models.
rationale.correct: The comparison states CM 'encompass[es] broader project coordination beyond quality verification' and 'address[es] schedule progression, cost control, multi-trade coordination, and resource management' while Supervision 'verifies contractor compliance without managing overall project coordination or cost control.'
rationale.takeaway: CM (SPP 204-B) adds schedule, cost control, and multi-trade coordination to supervision's quality focus—fundamentally different professional scopes and expertise.

questions.text: What does the comparison indicate about the relationship between service scope and compensation method?

options.text: Compensation methods align with service scope and professional responsibility intensity to establish value exchange
Compensation methods are established arbitrarily without relationship to service scope, often leading to inconsistencies in perceived value
All architectural services should use identical compensation regardless of scope, which simplifies billing but ignores project complexity
The comparison states that service scope has no impact on compensation determination, suggesting a one-size-fits-all approach

rationale.b: Denies systematic approach—the comparison explicitly establishes compensation as systematically aligned with service scope and responsibility.
rationale.c: Contradicts differentiation—the comparison identifies different compensation methods for different service scopes, not identical fees.
rationale.d: Contradicts direct statement—the comparison explicitly links scope and compensation as interconnected factors in service design.
rationale.correct: The comparison explicitly states 'Compensation methods align with service scope and professional responsibility intensity' and 'Clear fee structures prevent disputes and establish mutual understanding of value exchange.'
rationale.takeaway: Compensation directly reflects service scope and responsibility intensity—broader scope and greater responsibility justify higher or differently-structured fees than narrower services.

questions.text: What role does Design Administration play in the architect's overall project involvement according to the comparison?

options.text: Design Administration encompasses preliminary, design, construction, and post-construction services maintaining architect involvement across all phases
Design Administration only covers the design phase excluding construction and post-occupancy services, limiting the architect's role
The comparison indicates Design Administration has no relationship to other service categories, suggesting a standalone function
Design Administration is limited to construction phase supervision only, focusing on site activities and compliance

rationale.b: Incorrectly narrows scope—the comparison explicitly includes preliminary, construction, and post-construction services alongside design services.
rationale.c: Denies relationship—the comparison uses Design Administration to frame distinctions with supervision and CM services.
rationale.d: Overstates specialization—the comparison identifies Design Administration as spanning multiple phases beyond construction supervision.
rationale.correct: The comparison establishes Design Administration as 'the architect's involvement from concept through occupancy' and states it 'encompasses preliminary services, design phase services, construction phase services, and post-construction services.'
rationale.takeaway: Design Administration (SPP 202) maintains architect involvement across all project phases—preliminary, design, construction, post-occupancy—an integrated continuous engagement model.

questions.text: How do compensation methods differ among the three service models according to the comparison?

options.text: Supervision uses percentage or fixed fees; Construction Management uses percentage, hourly, or performance methods; Design Administration encompasses fees for entire project delivery
All three service models use identical percentage-of-cost compensation exclusively, without any variation for project type or complexity
The comparison indicates that compensation methods are unrelated to service scope, implying that the choice of method is arbitrary and not influenced by project specifics
SPP 202 Design Administration requires no separate compensation from supervision fees, as it is considered an integral part of the supervision process

rationale.b: Denies method variation—the comparison explicitly identifies different methods for each service type reflecting their different scopes.
rationale.c: Denies compensation logic—the comparison explicitly states compensation methods 'align with service scope and professional responsibility intensity.'
rationale.d: Confuses models—the comparison establishes Design Administration as a distinct comprehensive model with its own compensation framework, not supervision-based.
rationale.correct: The comparison states 'Full-time supervision typically employs percentage of construction cost or fixed fees'; 'Construction management uses percentage, hourly, or performance-based methods'; and 'Design administration encompasses fees for entire project delivery from concept through occupancy.'
rationale.takeaway: Each model has distinct compensation methods: Supervision (percentage/fixed fees), CM (percentage/hourly/performance), Design Admin (comprehensive project delivery fees)—aligned with service scope.

questions.text: According to the comparison framework, what is the primary focus of Full-Time Supervision services?

options.text: Quality control and design verification to ensure construction conforms to design specifications and technical standards
Comprehensive project delivery coordination including cost control and multi-trade scheduling, ensuring all aspects are aligned with the project timeline
Managing all project phases from concept through post-occupancy services, providing a holistic approach to project delivery
Replacing the contractor's responsibility for quality construction, which is not typically the role of supervision services

rationale.b: Confuses Supervision with Construction Management—the comparison explicitly states CM adds 'cost control and stakeholder management' beyond supervision's quality focus.
rationale.c: Confuses Supervision with Design Administration—the comparison identifies Design Administration (SPP 202) as the model spanning 'concept through occupancy,' not supervision.
rationale.d: Misunderstands the role—the comparison establishes supervision as verification and oversight, not assumption of contractor's construction responsibility.
rationale.correct: The comparison establishes that Full-Time Supervision focuses on 'quality control and design verification' ensuring 'materials, workmanship, and methods conform to design specifications and technical standards.'
rationale.takeaway: Full-Time Supervision (SPP 204-A) narrowly focuses on quality control and design verification during construction—not cost management or comprehensive project coordination.
